web_title: 6. 10-Year Financial Forensics, Cash Conversion & Capital Allocation
book_title: Chapter 6: The Ten-Year Ledger — Margins, Cash Conversion & ROIC
question: How have Arista's revenue, margins, working capital, stock-based compensation, cash conversion, and return on invested capital compounded from FY2016 through Q3 2026?

epigraph.quote: Profit is an opinion; cash is a fact.
epigraph.author: Alfred Rappaport (paraphrased)

web_blocks.title: 6.1 Ten-Year Income Statement & Cash Flow Forensics (FY2016–9M 2026)

web_blocks.html: From FY2016 through FY2025, Arista Networks grew annual revenue nearly eightfold from $1.13 billion to $9.01 billion [1][6]. That marks a 26.0% compound annual growth rate [1][6]. Growth then sped up 44.3% YoY to $9.40 billion in the first nine months of FY2026 [2]. Operating leverage was even stronger than top-line scale. GAAP operating income grew nearly sixteenfold from $243.5 million in FY2016 (21.5% margin) to $3,856.1 million in FY2025 (42.8% margin) [1][6]. In Q3 2026, operating margin reached 44.9% GAAP and 49.1% non-GAAP [3].

web_blocks.caption: Arista Networks: 10-Year Historical P&L, Margins & Cash Flow Forensics (FY2016–9M 2026)
web_blocks.takeaway: Revenue grew ~8x from FY2016 to FY2025 while GAAP operating margin doubled from 21.5% to 42.8%; FY2018 EBIT reflects the one-time $400M Cisco litigation settlement, and FY2022 CFO reflects proactive component inventory builds.

web_blocks.html: The ten-year ledger reveals three key forensic truths. First, gross margin stability stands out for a hardware-heavy vendor. Outside the 2022–2023 supply crunch (61.1%–62.0%), GAAP gross margin held between 63.8% and 64.5% in eight of ten years [1][6]. Second, R&D and SG&A discipline drove operating margin gains. As sales passed $9 billion, S&M and G&A fell as a share of revenue, while R&D stayed near 13%–14% [1]. Third, stock-based compensation (SBC) is tightly controlled compared with software peers. SBC fell from 6.3% of revenue in FY2021 to 4.9% ($439.2 million) in FY2025 [1][6]. That equaled just 10.3% of Free Cash Flow ($4,252.4 million) [1][6].

web_blocks.title: 6.2 Balance Sheet Fortress, Working Capital & ROIC

web_blocks.html: Arista carries zero financial debt, with Debt/Equity and LT Debt/Equity both at 0.00 [1]. At year-end 2025, cash ($1,963.9 million) and marketable securities ($8,779.1 million) totaled $10,743.0 million [1]. By September 30, 2026, that reserve grew to $14,359.0 million, split between $2,288.1 million in cash and $12,070.9 million in marketable securities [2]. Liquidity is ample, with a Current Ratio of 3.29 and a Quick Ratio of 2.82 [2]. That $14.36 billion cash pile earned $393.6 million in net other and interest income in FY2025 [1].

Working capital shifts explain both the 2022 cash dip and the 2024–2025 cash surge. In FY2022, Arista spent cash to build buffer inventory during the chip shortage [6]. That move cut CFO-to-Net-Income conversion to 36.5%, or $492.8 million CFO on $1,350.0 million net income [6]. Once supply chains cleared, inventory turned back into cash. CFO conversion rebounded to 130.2% in FY2024 ($3.71 billion CFO on $2.85 billion net income) [6]. In FY2025, conversion stayed strong at 124.5% ($4.37 billion CFO on $3.51 billion net income) [1]. At FY2025 year-end, Accounts Receivable stood at $1,886.9 million, or ~76 days DSO on $9,005.7 million in sales [1]. Inventories totaled $2,247.0 million (~253 days DIO on $3,237.0 million COGS), then rose to $3,210.0 million in Q3 2026 ahead of $3.9B–$4.0B Q4 shipments [1][2]. Accounts Payable ended FY2025 at $651.7 million, or ~73 days DPO [1].

web_blocks.takeaway: With 28.89% ROIC, 124.5% FY2025 CFO-to-Net-Income conversion, zero debt, and $1.6B in FY2025 share repurchases (3.6x SBC), Arista converts accounting earnings into owner-distributable cash at elite efficiency.

web_blocks.html: Capital return has been just as disciplined. Arista pays no cash dividend and instead returns excess cash through timely share buybacks [1]. In FY2025, it spent $1.6 billion on open-market repurchases [1]. That figure equaled 3.6x its $439.2 million SBC expense, so net share count shrank rather than diluted [1]. Its asset-light model earns a 28.89% Return on Invested Capital (ROIC) and 33.52% Return on Equity (ROE) even while holding $14.36 billion in cash. Together, these traits show textbook compounding economics.

book_paragraphs: Numbers over ten years strip away all storytelling. Look at Arista's ten-year ledger from 2016 through 2025, and you see one of the cleanest financial compounding records in modern technology hardware.

In 2016, Arista generated 1.13 billion dollars in revenue and 243.5 million dollars in GAAP operating profit—a 21.5 percent operating margin. By 2025, revenue had grown nearly eightfold to 9.01 billion dollars, a 26 percent compound annual growth rate, while GAAP operating profit expanded nearly sixteenfold to 3.86 billion dollars, doubling the operating margin to 42.8 percent. In the first nine months of 2026 alone, revenue reached 9.40 billion dollars, already surpassing all of 2025.

Even more revealing is how steady gross margins stayed across a decade of product transitions from 10G to 800G. Outside the 2022–2023 semiconductor crunch, when expedite fees pulled GAAP gross margin down to 61.1 percent, Arista held gross margins tightly between 63.8 and 64.5 percent for eight out of ten years.

book_subsections.title: Cash Conversion, Stock-Based Compensation, and Zero Debt
paragraphs: In tech investing, you always have to check whether accounting profits turn into real cash or vanish into stock-based compensation and working capital. In 2025, Arista's stock-based compensation was 439.2 million dollars—just 4.9 percent of revenue and barely 10 percent of Free Cash Flow. Meanwhile, the company repurchased 1.6 billion dollars of its own shares in 2025, wiping out SBC dilution more than three times over.

Working capital swings do happen. In 2022, Arista spent cash to stockpile scarce components, temporarily cutting operating cash flow conversion to 36.5 percent of net income. Once supply chains cleared, cash surged back: operating cash flow hit 130 percent of net income in 2024 and 124.5 percent in 2025, producing 4.25 billion dollars of Free Cash Flow.

On the balance sheet, Arista carries zero debt and held 14.36 billion dollars in cash and marketable securities at the end of September 2026. Even with that massive cash cushion sitting on the books, its Return on Invested Capital stands at 28.89 percent—nearly three times any reasonable cost of capital.

callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
callouts.text: When you and I finish a price-blind audit of Arista Networks, the verdict on business quality is unambiguous. It combines software-level margins and 28.89 percent ROIC with an eighteen-year owner-oriented CEO and a debt-free 14.36-billion-dollar balance sheet. The only reasons to stay vigilant are structural: 42 percent customer concentration in Microsoft and Meta, NVIDIA's bundled Spectrum-X push, and 11.4 billion dollars in binding purchase commitments.

book_subsections.title: Ten-Year Forensic Proof: Quality of Earnings and Capital Efficiency
paragraphs: Across a full ten-year arc from FY2016 through Q3 2026, Arista's financial statements read like a textbook case of high-ROIC compounding. Revenue expanded nearly eightfold from $1.13 billion in FY2016 to $9.01 billion in FY2025 before accelerating 44.3% in the first nine months of 2026. Over that same decade, GAAP operating margins more than doubled from 21.5% to 42.8% (reaching 44.9% in Q3 2026) because R&D and sales expenses scaled far more slowly than revenue.

More importantly, those accounting profits are backed by real cash. In FY2025, cash flow from operations reached $4.37 billion—124.5% of GAAP net income—and free cash flow hit $4.25 billion, a 47.2% free cash flow margin. Stock-based compensation stayed disciplined at 4.9% of revenue ($439.2 million), well below typical Silicon Valley software peers, allowing share buybacks to more than offset dilution. With $14.36 billion in cash and marketable securities and zero debt on the balance sheet, Arista enters any potential industry downturn from a position of extraordinary financial strength.

book_subsections.title: How Zero Debt and Disciplined Buybacks Compound Per-Share Value
paragraphs: Many high-growth technology companies flatter their non-GAAP profits by handing out massive stock-based compensation—often 15% to 25% of revenue—which quietly dilutes shareholders unless the company burns cash buying back shares. Arista stands apart. In FY2025, stock-based compensation totaled $439.2 million, or just 4.9% of revenue, while free cash flow reached $4.25 billion.

Because Arista carries zero long-term debt and earns interest on $14.36 billion of cash and marketable securities, every dollar of free cash flow belongs to equity owners. Management uses opportunistic share repurchases to shrink the share count over time and keeps plenty of liquidity on hand to fund supply-chain commitments during 58% growth surges without ever tapping debt markets.

book_subsections.title: Balance Sheet Fortress: Why $14.36 Billion in Net Cash Matters
paragraphs: In a cyclical technology downturn, debt turns a temporary revenue pause into an existential crisis. Arista carries zero short-term or long-term debt against $14.36 billion in cash and marketable securities as of September 30, 2026. That fortress balance sheet does three things for owners: it earns hundreds of millions in annual interest income at 4% to 5% Treasury yields, it lets Arista guarantee supply-chain commitments to win massive hyperscaler contracts, and it gives management dry powder to repurchase shares whenever market corrections create bargains.

book_subsections.title: Why Cash Flow Quality Beats Headline EPS
paragraphs: Headline earnings per share can always be massaged by aggressive revenue recognition or capitalized expenses, which is why serious owners check cash conversion first. Across FY2021 through FY2025, Arista's cumulative operating cash flow consistently matched or exceeded GAAP net income, culminating in 124.5% conversion in FY2025. When cash in the bank grows faster than reported accounting profit, earnings quality is high.
